title: Domain Name System (DNS) Case Insensitivity Clarification
summary: DNS names are case insensitive, and this document spells out exactly what that means by giving clear rules for how letters are compared. It updates RFC 1034, RFC 1035, and RFC 2181. It is a standards-track clarification rather than a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: WWW.Example.COM and www.example.com lead to the same place. This explains the exact rules for treating big and small letters as the same in internet names.

questions: how does dns compare domain names
dns escape sequences for special characters
subtitle: The exact rules for how DNS treats uppercase and lowercase letters as equivalent.

tldr.problem: DNS specification said names are case insensitive, but did not clearly explain what that means for comparisons, output, and special characters.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies that ASCII letters (A-Z and a-z) must match case-insensitively during DNS lookups, with exact rules for case folding and preservation, and clarifies that non-ASCII bytes do not follow case rules.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can now write DNS software with certainty about how to compare names and preserve case correctly.

today: RFC 4343 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2006 and clarifies earlier DNS standards. It updates RFC 1034, RFC 1035, and RFC 2181. It was itself updated by RFC 5890 in 2010. The rules it establishes remain the foundation for DNS name comparison and case handling today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the global distributed database for internet addressing and mail routing. DNS names consist of labels separated by periods, such as www.example.com. The original DNS specification said these names are treated in a case-insensitive way, but did not clearly define what that means.

RFC 4343 clarifies the exact meaning of case insensitivity for DNS. The document updates three earlier RFCs: RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 (the original DNS standards, now grouped as STD 13) and RFC 2181 (which clarified some DNS details).
sections.plainLanguage: DNS lets you type domain names in any mix of uppercase and lowercase, and they all work the same. But what exactly does that mean? This RFC explains the rules precisely.

sections.title: Case Insensitivity of DNS Labels
sections.content:
According to DNS design, name lookups must be case insensitive. That means a lookup string containing an uppercase ASCII letter (0x41 to 0x5A, the letters A-Z) MUST match the identical value and also match the corresponding lowercase ASCII letter (0x61 to 0x7A, the letters a-z). The reverse is also true: a lowercase letter must match itself and the corresponding uppercase letter.

One way to implement this is case folding: subtracting 0x20 from all lowercase letters before comparison. However, the implementation method is not prescribed. Importantly, DNS case insensitivity does NOT use the case folding rules defined in ISO 8859-1 or ISO 8859-2. For example, the bytes 0xDD and 0xFD, which might represent uppercase and lowercase versions of Y with an accent in those character sets, do NOT match in DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: When comparing domain names, A matches a, B matches b, and so on through Z matching z. But the rules only apply to the English alphabet letters, not to any other special characters.

sections.title: Escaping Unusual Label Octets
sections.content:
DNS labels are 8-bit bytes, not limited to ASCII characters. When writing DNS names in human-readable form (Master Files), certain bytes must be escaped: the period (0x2E, ".") and all bytes outside the printable ASCII range (all values from 0x00 to 0x20 and from 0x7F to 0xFF).

The convention is to use a backslash followed by exactly three decimal digits. For example, a space (0x20) is written as \032, and a period is written as \046 or \. A backslash itself is written as \092 or \\. Example labels include Donald\032E\.\032Eastlake\0323rd (which contains spaces and a period) and a\000\\\255z (which contains a null byte, a backslash, and a byte with all bits set).
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters (like periods and control codes) can't be typed normally in DNS names, so we write them as backslash followed by three numbers. This lets you put unusual characters in names if needed.

sections.title: Label Types and CLASS
sections.content:
DNS labels in wire-encoded messages have a type. The original DNS standard had two types: ASCII labels (length zero to 63 octets) and indirect labels (compression pointers). ASCII labels follow the case insensitivity rules described here. Indirect labels are replaced by the name to which they point, and that name is then treated with case insensitivity rules.

DNS was later extended (by RFC 2671) to allow additional label types. The only such type defined so far is BINARY (RFC 2673, now Experimental). The ASCII case insensitivity rules apply only to ASCII labels (type 0x0), not to other label types.

DNS also has an additional dimension called CLASS (for example, the Internet (IN) class). The handling of label case is not CLASS-dependent. Case insensitivity is uniform across all classes.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS can use different label types for different purposes. Case insensitivity only applies to regular ASCII labels, not to special label types.

sections.title: Case Preservation on Input and Output
sections.content:
While ASCII label comparisons are case insensitive, the DNS specification says case MUST be preserved on output and preserved when convenient on input. However, this is less absolute than it sounds.

On output, DNS marshals names by walking up the name tree and outputting each label encountered, without doing case conversion. This preserves case. However, DNS optimization through indirect labels (name compression) can destroy case preservation. When the output code determines that a name tail matches another name for the purpose of compression, it uses case-insensitive comparison, so the output may use either capitalization.

On input, when DNS data comes from a Master File, zone transfer, dynamic update, or incremental zone transfer, no case conversion is done when creating new nodes. The case of ASCII labels is preserved. However, when inputting a name for a node that already exists, implementations are free to retain the original case, allow new input to override it, or maintain separate copies. This means that two A records under "foo.bar.example" and "FOO.BAR.example" might be returned with either capitalization, or even a mixture, depending on implementation and name compression.
sections.plainLanguage: When you store a domain name, DNS remembers the uppercase and lowercase letters you typed. But when it compares names or sends them in answers, it might change the case or use name compression, so you might not see the same capitalization you put in.

sections.title: Internationalized Domain Names
sections.content:
A separate scheme for internationalized domain names (IDN) and internationalized labels has been developed (RFC 3490, RFC 3454, RFC 3491, RFC 3492). This scheme makes Unicode available through an application-level transformation between internationalized domain names and DNS domain names.

Any case insensitivity in internationalized domain names depends on the script (alphabet) used and is handled entirely by the transformation process described in RFC 3454 and RFC 3491, not by DNS itself. This is separate from the standard DNS as defined in STD 13.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to use domain names in non-English languages, there is a separate system that turns them into regular DNS names. Case rules for those languages are handled in that translation system, not in DNS.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The equivalence of DNS labels that differ only in case can lead to security problems. A user could be confused by thinking two domain names differing only in case were different.

Domain names may also be used outside the DNS, such as as a case-sensitive index into a database or file system, or interpreted as binary data by integrity or authentication code systems. These problems can usually be handled by using a standardized canonical form of DNS ASCII labels, always mapping ASCII letter octets to a specific pre-chosen case (either uppercase or lowercase).

Another risk is storing non-DNS names (such as case-sensitive email address local parts) into DNS with the expectation that case will be preserved. On a system with case-sensitive email local parts, storing two Responsible Person (RP) records differing only in case could produce unexpected results with security implications, since the entire email address, including the possibly case-sensitive local part, is encoded into a DNS name where case might change on output.
sections.plainLanguage: Since DNS treats uppercase and lowercase the same, criminals might try to trick people by using tricky capitalization. Also, if you store case-sensitive things (like some email addresses) in DNS, the case might not stay the same, which could break things.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
Implementers should be aware that the DNS case insensitivity rules are simple: only ASCII letters A-Z and a-z participate, with a match when they differ only in case. All other bytes do not participate in case rules.

For case preservation in output, implementers should not assume that case will be preserved across name compression or multiple inputs. A canonical representation (such as all lowercase or all uppercase) is recommended for security-critical operations that use DNS names.

When implementing IDN (internationalized domain names), remember that case handling for non-ASCII scripts is part of the IDN transformation, not part of DNS itself.
sections.plainLanguage: When writing DNS software, remember that only English letters have case rules, and case gets mixed up when DNS compresses names. Use all-lowercase or all-uppercase as a standard form for important security checks.
